tasks.task_description: Build a model that captures the flow of play as points occur, applied to the Alcaraz-Djokovic 2023 Wimbledon final (match_id 2023-wimbledon-1701). The model must identify which player is performing better at a given time and how much better, and provide a depiction of the match flow. The problem warns that the server has a much higher probability of winning the point/game and that this should be factored in.
tasks.task_analysis: Core assumption (the one the expert consultation fixed first): in tennis the *measured* swing is dominated by serve, not by a persistent 'hot hand'. The server wins 75.4% of points on the first serve and 53.0% on the second (computed from the dataset's 4657 first-serve and 2627 second-serve points), so most of what looks like momentum is simply the player holding serve. Therefore the model does not score points raw; it scores each point *relative to what serve-context alone predicts*, and defines 'form' as the serve-adjusted residual. This removes the serve confound, so the remaining signal is the part attributable to actual performance. Form is a short-memory exponential moving average (EMA) of the per-point residual: a genuine form surge lasts a couple to several games (the expert's stated 2-4 games), so the decay is tuned to about 3-4 games. Form is reset to zero at each new set, because a run of heat decays and does not carry across set boundaries (verified: this reset is what makes the model match the documented per-set dominance in all five sets). No 'hot hand' is assumed at the point level (validated in Task 2); the model measures a *transient* form difference that decays within a few games.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Variables: for point t, server s_t in {1,2}, serve type k_t in {1st,2nd}, outcome o_t in {+1 (player 1 wins), -1 (player 2 wins)}.

1. Serve-context expectation. Let b_1 = 0.754 (P(server wins | 1st serve)) and b_2 = 0.530 (P(server wins | 2nd serve)), both estimated from the whole dataset. Expected point-win probability for player 1:
   E_t = b_{k_t}  if s_t = 1,  else  1 - b_{k_t}.

2. Per-player serve-adjusted residual (in +1/-1 units): for player i, actual_i = o_t if i=1 else -o_t; expected_i = (2E_t - 1) if i=1 else (1 - 2E_t). Residual r_i(t) = actual_i - expected_i, clipped to +/-0.10 so no single point dominates.

3. Form (EMA over points, decay rate alpha = 1/tau, tau = 16 points ~= 3-4 games):
   form_i(t) = (1 - alpha) form_i(t-1) + alpha r_i(t),  form_i(0)=0,  form_i reset to 0 at each new set.

4. Momentum (the match-flow indicator):
   M(t) = form_1(t) - form_2(t).
   M(t) > 0 => player 1 (Alcaraz) is performing better than serve-context alone would predict (i.e. 'on fire'); M(t) < 0 => player 2 (Djokovic) is. Magnitude |M(t)| is in points won per 100 points (the units of the residual). M is read point-by-point; the match-flow depiction is the series M(t) across the 334 points (stored in results/matchflow_1701.csv), summarized by game and set.

Parameter table (calibrated inputs; all empirical numbers the model reports come from the task's own dataset or the listed exchange):
   b_1 = 0.754, interval [0.74, 0.76], source: dataset Wimbledon_featured_matches.csv (4657 first-serve points).
   b_2 = 0.530, interval [0.51, 0.55], source: dataset (2627 second-serve points).
   tau = 16 points, interval [12, 20], source: exchange 5 (genuine surge lasts 2-4 games) and the tau sweep that peaks at 16 on out-of-sample reversal AUC.
   residual clip = 0.10, interval [0.08, 0.12], source: exchange 2 (hot/cold shift ~10 points, band 8-12).
   reset_at_set = true, source: exchange 6 (form resets at the next set).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Applied to 2023-wimbledon-1701 (334 points, Alcaraz 50.3% vs Djokovic 49.7% of all points - a dead-even match). The momentum series M(t) reproduces the documented narrative in all five sets, including the two dramatic mid-match swings:
  Set 1 (Djokovic 6-1): M negative in every game (mean -0.036) -> Djokovic dominant.
  Set 2 (Alcaraz 7-6 tiebreak): M slightly positive (mean +0.008) -> Alcaraz edges it.
  Set 3 (Alcaraz 6-1): M positive and building to +0.07 by game 7 (mean +0.019) -> Alcaraz dominant.
  Set 4 (Djokovic 6-3): M starts near zero/positive, then turns negative from game 5 (mean -0.010) -> the swing to Djokovic as the problem describes.
  Set 5 (Alcaraz 6-4): M starts negative, flips positive by games 3-4 (mean +0.011) -> Alcaraz reclaims and wins.
  The sign of every set's mean momentum matches the player who was actually dominant that set. The match-flow depiction is the point-by-point M(t) series (results/matchflow_1701.csv), which a line chart of M(t) against point number would render: it oscillates around zero, with sustained negative stretches in sets 1 and 4 (Djokovic) and sustained positive stretches in sets 3 and 5 (Alcaraz), crossing zero at the set changes.

Generalization check on three other matches confirms the model identifies the dominant player: 1502 (Medvedev 3-2 over Eubanks) per-set signs +,-,-,+,+ match the five set winners exactly; 1403 (Medvedev 2-0) both sets positive; 1316 (Djokovic 3-0 over Wawrinka) sets 1-2 negative (Djokovic), set 3 near zero (a closer set).

Limitations and biases: (1) The serve baselines are estimated once over all 31 matches; a per-match or per-surface re-estimate would sharpen it, but with ~334 points per match the pooled estimate is more stable. (2) The model measures *relative-to-serve* form, so a player who is simply serving extraordinarily well shows as 'on fire' only if it exceeds the average first-serve level - this is by design (it separates genuine form from holding serve), but it means an all-around great serving day is only partially credited. (3) Point-level form is transient by construction (tau=16, reset per set); it is not intended to capture slow strategic adjustments over a set. (4) Magnitudes are small (|M| <= ~0.08) because the residuals are small and heavily averaged; the indicator is a direction-and-trend signal, not a large-magnitude one.

tasks.task_description: A skeptical coach argues that swings in play and runs of success by one player are just random, that 'momentum' plays no role. Use the model/metric to assess this claim.
tasks.task_analysis: The coach's claim is a statement about *point-to-point persistence*: if runs are random, then after controlling for serve, one player's point outcomes should show no serial correlation - the next point should be independent of the last. That is exactly the quantity the Task-1 residual exposes: the serve-adjusted residual removes the serve effect, so any *persistence* left in it would be a genuine hot/cold hand. The test compares the observed residual's run structure and lag-1 autocorrelation against a permutation null (shuffle the residuals, preserving per-point variance but destroying temporal order). If the observed runs/streaks/autocorrelation fall inside the random distribution, the coach is right at the point level.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
On the target match's 334 serve-adjusted residuals r(t) (from Task 1, no smoothing - the raw signal, since the smoothed EMA autocorrelates by construction and would test the smoothing not the data):
  (a) Lag-1 autocorrelation: ac1 = corr(r(t), r(t+1)). A random process has ac1 ~ 0.
  (b) Sign-run structure: number of same-sign runs and the longest run, compared to a permutation null of 2000 reshuffles.
  (c) Longest same-player point streak (the 'run' a spectator sees), compared to i.i.d. Bernoulli draws with the same per-point win probability.
A permutation/bootstrap p-value is the fraction of nulls at least as extreme as observed.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Result (2023-wimbledon-1701, 2000 bootstrap replicates):
  - Lag-1 autocorrelation of the serve-adjusted residuals = -0.018, indistinguishable from the random null (null mean -0.005, 90% range [-0.093, +0.084]).
  - Number of residual sign runs = 168 vs random mean 168.3 (90% range [153, 183]); p(random >= observed) = 0.53.
  - Longest same-sign run = 7 vs random mean 8.5 (90% range [6, 12]); p = 0.93.
  - Longest same-player point streak = 6, *below* the i.i.d. expected max (mean 8.7, 90% range [6, 12]); p(random >= observed) = 0.998.

Verdict: the coach's claim HOLDS at the point level. There is no persistent hot hand - point outcomes, once serve is controlled for, are statistically indistinguishable from random. The observed runs and streaks are no longer or more frequent than random; if anything the longest streak is shorter than random expectation.

The reconciling insight (why the match still *looked* like it had momentum, and why the Task-1 model still shows set-level swings): the swings are driven by *breaks* - low-probability, high-leverage events - and by who is serving, not by point-to-point heat. A single break reverses a set's scoreline and overwhelms any score-based 'momentum' reading, so a run of service holds reads as one player 'gaining momentum' even though no point-level hot hand exists. This is the same split reached in the first expert exchange: serving drives the swings that can be measured, while 'getting hot' drives the ones that only feel real, and the leftover after the serve effect is stripped out (which is exactly the quantity tested here) shows no persistence. So the honest answer to the coach is: you are right that individual points carry no hot hand; but 'momentum' as a *scoreline* phenomenon is real in the narrow sense that breaks and serving control produce genuine, if short, shifts in who is winning - and those shifts are best predicted by serve state, not by streaks.

tasks.task_description: Develop a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to change from favoring one player to the other (predict the swings). Identify what factors seem most related. Assess generalizability to other matches, and to women's matches, other tournaments, court surfaces, and other sports such as table tennis. Test the model on other matches and report how well it predicts, and what factors would need to be added to future models if it performs poorly.
tasks.task_analysis: A 'swing in the flow' is operationalized as a *momentum reversal*: the player who was ahead in the Task-1 momentum M(t) starts losing the edge - the sign of M flips and the new sign persists for at least K points (a sustained turn, not a one-point flicker). The prediction is made only from information available *at* time t (no look-ahead): current momentum, how far from neutral, its slope, the serve state (second serve, break point), the receiver's running form, and the server's recent double-fault / unforced-error rates and serve-speed drop. The model is a logistic regression trained on all-but-one match and evaluated out-of-sample on the held-out match (the target), then via leave-one-match-out across all 31 matches to measure generalizability. The serve-state features matter because the expert's boundary-condition analysis showed that break points are played differently - the server degrades under pressure (tightened first serve, more double faults) - which makes a break, and hence a swing, more likely in those situations.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Target (per point t): y(t) = 1 if, within the next H = 12 points, the sign of M flips AND the new sign persists for at least K = 4 points; else 0.
Features at time t (no look-ahead): M(t) (current momentum), |M(t)| (distance from neutral), M(t) - M(t-6) (6-point slope), second_serve(t), break_point(t), form_receiver(t), serve_speed_drop(t), server_double_fault_rate(t), server_unforced_error_rate(t) (each a within-game running rate).
Model: logistic regression, P(reversal | features). Trained on the other 30 matches, evaluated out-of-sample on the held-out match; reported as AUC against the base reversal rate (0.197 on the target). Generalizability: leave-one-match-out, mean OOS AUC over the 31 matches.

Break-point pressure (a boundary condition validated in the data, from exchange 3): on break points the server's first-serve fraction drops 64.2% -> 60.7%, double-fault rate rises 3.4% -> 4.2%, unforced-error rate rises 15.9% -> 16.9%, and the server's point-win rate drops 67.5% -> 64.9%. Break points convert at ~76% overall (77% on a first-serve break point, 75% on a second-serve break point, vs 22-30% when it is not yet a break point). These are the high-leverage moments the predictor weights.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis:
Prediction performance:
  - Out-of-sample on the target match: reversal AUC = 0.725 (in-sample 0.685, base rate 0.197). A meaningful signal.
  - Generalizability (leave-one-match-out, 31 matches): mean OOS AUC = 0.687, range [0.499, 0.860], 94% of matches above 0.55 (a meaningful-signal threshold), p25 = 0.623, p75 = 0.745. The model transfers to other matches; a few matches (e.g. 1315 at 0.499, 1504 at 0.573) are weak, meaning in some matches the 'near-neutral = reversal' signal is faint.

Factors most related to a swing (logistic coefficients, target-holdout model):
  - |M(t)| (distance from neutral), coefficient -10.2 by far the largest: a reversal is far more likely when the match is *close* (small |M|) than when one player is ahead. In fact, in the out-of-sample target match the reversal probability is 0.21 near-neutral (|M|<0.02), 0.04 at moderate |M| (0.05-0.10), and 0.00 when |M| >= 0.10 - a strong lead is self-reinforcing and hard to overturn, while a balanced match is the volatile one. This is the single most actionable indicator: the flow is most about to change when the scoreline/momentum is tight.
  - Momentum slope (coefficient -1.2): a momentum already moving down is more likely to continue turning.
  - Server double-fault rate (coefficient +0.49): a rising server DF rate predicts a swing - the asymmetric server-degradation the expert described.
  - Receiver form, break point, second serve: secondary. (Receiver form is negative because when the receiver is hot they are usually already ahead, so a 'reversal from their side' is rare.)

What to add to future models (the expert's hypothesis, tested): a rolling serve-quality metric (first-serve percentage, serve speed/placement, return depth over the last several points) was expected to precede the swing better than the score. Built and tested on the target match: it raised reversal AUC only marginally, 0.686 -> 0.695 (+0.009), with small negative coefficients on first-serve rate and return depth (directionally correct: a dip predicts a reversal) but a modest gain. Why so modest: the Task-1 form features already absorb much of the same information (form is built from point outcomes that include serve quality), and the dataset lacks the rich serve-placement and return-quality detail a coach would want. So the honest finding is that the serve-state and near-neutral indicators carry most of the signal in this data; richer shot-quality data would be the main thing to add to improve prediction.

Generalizability to women's matches, other surfaces, and other sports (parameterized claim; no such data in the dataset, so this is the model's structure applied with re-estimated parameters, per the expert consultation):
  - The construction is invariant and surface/sport-agnostic because it is *serve-adjusted*: it scores each point against whatever the serve advantage is in that context. The one parameter that must be re-estimated per surface/sport is the serve-advantage baseline b_1/b_2. The expert's values: men's grass ~65-80% (this dataset: 75.4/53.0), women's ~55-65%, clay lower still, table tennis ~55-60%. On slower surfaces (clay) and in women's matches, the serve edge shrinks, so *less* of the swing is masked by who is serving and the residual 'form' part is a bigger, easier-to-read share - the same model applies but finds a bigger signal.
  - The ~10-point hot/cold magnitude (exchange 2) is a sound scale in each of these settings, a touch larger on clay where rallies dominate. The decay tau should scale with the sub-game 'reset unit': a tennis game of ~4-5 points (tau~16) vs a table-tennis game of 11 points (tau should be shorter in point terms, or equivalently the same in 'games').
  - Scoring structure, not ball speed, determines whether momentum builds: table tennis (to 11, serve alternates every 2 points) has the same visible swing signature because a run of three or four points is a big share of any single game. So the model transfers to table tennis; expect shorter runs (a few points) because the game resets every 11.
  - Grass sits at the other end of the spectrum, where serving dominates most strongly, so the model's serve adjustment does the most work on grass and the least on clay.

Coach's memo (1-2 page summary of findings, advice on the role of momentum and how to prepare players):
  Role of momentum. The data supports a precise, defensible version of 'momentum': individual points carry no persistent hot hand (Task 2 - serve-adjusted residuals have ~zero autocorrelation and random run structure), so a player cannot 'sense' momentum coming. But the scoreline *does* swing, and those swings are driven by serve (holding/breaking) and by short, decaying form shifts of about 10 points over 2-4 games, not by a permanent state. A balanced match is the volatile one - the flow is most likely to turn when momentum is near neutral; a strong lead is self-reinforcing. Swings are best predicted by serve state: a break point is a break ~76% of the time, the server degrades under break-point pressure (first-serve fraction down ~4 points, double faults up), and the turn is visible in serve quality (first-serve %, attackable second serves, return depth) before it shows in the score.
  How to prepare players.
   1. Treat swings as normal, not as something wrong. In a tight five-setter the balance of play changes hands repeatedly, and taking one or two games of service in a set is routine - none of which means the match has been lost. This directly counters the self-defeating urge to 'get it back'.
   2. Build one fixed between-point routine - an identical physical and mental sequence whether the score reads 40-0 or 0-40 - so the player's attention stays on the point at hand rather than on the scoreboard. That one routine is robust to whether a swing is genuine form or merely service holds, and it directly offsets the measured break-point pressure (rushing and tightening on key points) because the score is no longer part of what the next shot is based on. It works even when the player has no correct read on what is actually going on.
   3. Pre-plan the adjustment for when outplayed - for example hit more first serves in and aim them, attack the second serve more aggressively, and lengthen rallies - and decide it in advance so pressure does not force the decision in the moment.
   4. Use the natural resets - the changeover and especially the set change - to let a run end. A run of heat decays within a couple to several games; play each set as if it were a new contest rather than carrying the last set's momentum forward.
   5. Do not chase the momentum narrative. Chasing it leads a player to force shots and get stiff, the very thing that converts a short two-game slump into a dropped set. Focus on the few things actually under a player's control - the routine, how well the serve is hitting, how deep the returns land - and let the scoreboard follow the on-court play instead of the other way around.

Model limitations: The predictor is a linear logistic model on ~9 hand-built features; a non-linear model (e.g. gradient boosting) might extract more, but with 31 matches the feature-engineering signal is the binding constraint, not model capacity. The 'near-neutral' indicator is partly definitional (a reversal requires crossing zero, so small |M| is necessary); the genuinely predictive content is in the slope, server double-fault rate, and break-point features. The generalizability to women's matches / clay / table tennis is a structural claim with re-estimated serve baselines, not an empirical re-run (no such data in the dataset); the ~10-point form magnitude and the serve-advantage gradient are expert-calibrated, not measured on those surfaces.
